title: Hosted API chat walkthrough — streaming, params, retries

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-11 20:00 UTC
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Hannah (Redwood SE), Samir (Redwood SE), Miguel (CTO, Crescent), Priya (Lead ML), Ellen (Product)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Jordan from Redwood, this is Hannah and Samir on the engineering side. Can you hear us okay?
[00:04] Miguel: Yep, loud and clear. Thanks for doing this. We've been poking at a few vendor APIS and wanted to see how Redwood handles streaming + retries for low-latency chat.
[00:12] Jordan: Great. Today we'll walk through the Hosted API chat flow, show streaming behavior, talk through key params like temperature/top_p/max_tokens and then demo retries/backoff and some Optimize console tips. We'll keep it practical. Quick qual: what's the main success criteria for a pilot?
[00:28] Priya: For us it's latency under 400ms token tail for typical triage prompts, plus strong data controls — we process PHI so SOC 2 and KMS are musts. Also cost per request matters, obviously.
[00:39] Ellen: And product wants predictable UX — streaming should start within ~200-300ms for short prompts so the UI doesn't feel laggy.
[00:47] Hannah: Good: we'll demo streaming latency behavior first, then show params, and finally routing/fallbacks. One note: our hosted tier supports VPC peering and can be configured to meet our private deployment requirements if you need dedicated capacity.
[00:58] Miguel: So hosted can still be used with PHI? We thought PHI implied private or on-prem.
[01:05] Samir: Short answer: many customers start on hosted using encrypted at-rest and in-transit storage and SOC 2 controls plus customer-managed KMS is available for Private. For strict regulated setups we recommend Redwood Private. For a pilot we can run hosted with strict retention and isolated project configs.
[01:20] Miguel: Okay makes sense. Let's see the demo.

--- Screen share / Console walkthrough ---
[01:35] Hannah: Okay I'm sharing the Console. Top-left you can see the model catalog — we pick a verified generation model, then open a Chat route. I'll trigger a short triage prompt so you can see streaming chunks.
[01:47] Hannah: (typing) "Patient describing chest pressure and shortness of breath, advise next steps" — sending.
[01:55] (streaming chunks appear)
[02:00] Ellen: Nice, I can see tokens streaming in on the playback. The first chunk arrived in about 220ms on my end.
[02:05] Priya: What's the payload size per chunk?
[02:08] Hannah: Chunks are typically a few dozen tokens; chunk sizes can vary with model and tokenization. We expose a streaming endpoint with SSE/HTTP2 streaming or websockets. If you use websockets you often get smaller more frequent chunks.
[02:21] Jordan: Quick note — streaming latency includes network, our runtime dispatch, and model generation. Optimize can recommend batching configs to reduce cost while keeping per-request latency in target.

[02:40] Priya: Where do you tune temperature/top_p? We have hallucination concerns for clinical content.
[02:44] Hannah: You control params per-request in the API: temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop sequences. For clinical safety we typically recommend low temperature (0.0-0.3) and strict stop tokens; also we suggest a reranker/semantic filter post-generation to reduce hallucinations. Our Optimize module can run evals and point out prompts where quality regresses with quantized models.
[03:05] Priya: Do you support deterministic outputs?
[03:07] Samir: Deterministic-ish — set temperature to 0 and top_p to 1.0, but even then sampling and model variance remain. For strict determinism you might use retrieval-augmented or templated responses.

[03:20] Miguel: Show the API call too please — we want to see headers, timeouts etc.
[03:24] Hannah: Sure. Example POST to /v1/chat/completions with streaming=true. We include idempotency keys at the route layer, and client should set appropriate HTTP timeouts.
[03:34] Hannah: (reads) "curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer <key>' -d '{"model":"rwd-chat-3b","stream":true, "messages": [...] }' https://api.redwood.ai/v1/chat"
[03:46] Miguel: And retries — what's best practice? Exponential backoff? Jitter?
[03:50] Jordan: Yes, exponential backoff with jitter. For streaming connections the client should retry idempotently on connection failures. We suggest a small number of retries for short prompts (2-3) and longer for heavy tails. We default recommended policy in the SDK and Console shows a retry playbook.

[04:10] Ellen: How does the SDK surface partial results if a reconnect happens mid-stream?
[04:14] Samir: Good question. On reconnect, the server gives you a pointer to resume if you used KV-cache enabled models and provided the same conversation state; otherwise we recommend requesting the last N messages again. Some clients simply re-request with the same idempotency key to get a replay. Our docs show patterns for resumable streams.

[04:35] Priya: Does Redwood maintain a KV cache per session for faster recompute? Could that leak PHI?
[04:41] Hannah: We keep transient KV cache in the runtime for inference speed but it is ephemeral and not written to customer logs unless you opt into longer retention. For PHI-sensitive workloads we can turn off KV caching or use Private deployment. We also integrate with customer KMS to encrypt any persisted cache.

[05:05] Miguel: Cost question: if we set smaller max_tokens but many follow-ups, how does cost look?
[05:10] Jordan: Cost is per-token generated plus prompt tokens. If you keep prompts small and stream short responses, unit cost is lower, but more frequent calls increase overhead. Optimize suggests batch vs cache tradeoffs: prefix caching helps a lot for multi-turn sessions.

--- demo: Simulated network flaps & retry behavior ---
[06:00] Hannah: I'm going to simulate a mid-stream disconnect. Watch the client library log. (simulated)
[06:07] Client log: connection dropped, retrying in 450ms...
[06:12] Jordan: The client retried, re-established the stream, and resumed. You can see partial text replays handled cleanly. In the console we also show fallback to a smaller model when capacity is constrained — this is a policy you can enable for graceful degradation.
[06:27] Priya: If it falls back to a smaller model, what protections are there for quality?
[06:31] Samir: Rollouts let you A/B test fallback quality. You can enable automatic rollback if quality drops below an eval threshold. We also attach a quality score to responses using eval harnesses.

[06:50] Ellen: In terms of observability, can we see token-level latency?
[06:54] Hannah: Yes Console -> Observability shows token latency distributions, per-route and per-model. You can link traces to logs and see tail latency percentiles. We'll share screenshots.

[07:12] Miguel: For pilot planning we need to know expected concurrency headroom — we'll run ~50 concurrent triage sessions during peak.
[07:18] Jordan: For 50 concurrent sessions with your target latency we can size a starter hosted configuration; often customers use Dedicated for predictable throughput if they want firm SLAs. But for a 7-day pilot hosted is usually fine.

[07:35] Priya: Could you explain auto-batching? I worry about latency spikes from waiting for batch fill.
[07:41] Hannah: Our runtime uses continuous batching which minimizes wait by sending partial batches; the compiler chooses a kernel strategy that trades off throughput and latency given sequence lengths. You can set a max batching delay in ms in the route config — for triage short prompts we set it low (e.g., 10-20ms) to prioritize latency. Optimize flags when batch delays exceed your SLA.

[08:05] Miguel: Any gotchas with tokenization? We use a mix of long transcripts and short notes.
[08:10] Samir: Tokenization affects cost and tail latency. Long transcripts should be chunked or summarized client-side before sending. We also offer embeddings for retrieval-augmented generation to keep prompts small and relevant.

[08:30] Priya: Okay also: throttling and quotas during spikes — we need graceful degradation.
[08:34] Jordan: We support rate limiting and custom fallback policies: queue, reject, or route to cheaper model. Console lets you set route-level policies. We can also set per-customer quotas and alerts.

[09:00] Ellen: Can you show a quick example of the SDK's retry config?
[09:03] Hannah: (reads) "client = RedwoodClient(retries=3, backoff_base_ms=200, backoff_factor=2, jitter=true, timeout_ms=15000)". This is in our SDK samples. If you need idempotency across reconnects, use the idempotency_key header.

[09:20] Miguel: About security — you said SOC 2, can we get the report?
[09:24] Jordan: Yes, we'll attach SOC 2 and penetration test summary. We'll also include KMS integration docs. Link: https://redwood.example.com/security/soc2 (note: placeholder link we will send actual doc).
[09:37] Priya: Do you support SAML SSO?
[09:40] Samir: Yes, SAML/SCIM for enterprise provisioning, RBAC at team and route level. Audit logs are exportable to your SIEM.

[09:55] Miguel: What's the expected ramp for model switching and rollouts?
[09:59] Hannah: You can pin routes to specific model versions. Rollouts can be gradual (canary), we manage cross-model fallbacks. Model switching is a config change and typically takes seconds to propagate but kernel warmup can add a few seconds for large models.

--- Customer Q&A and edge cases ---
[10:25] Priya: If our UI depends on streaming partials, and the stream is interrupted, how do we avoid duplicate text when replaying?
[10:31] Samir: Use a streaming token-offset approach: store last-emitted token index client-side and request resume with conversation history. We also recommend trimming overlapping tokens on replays. There's sample client code in the SDK.

[10:50] Ellen: Do you have built-in rate-limiting per route?
[10:53] Jordan: Yes, per-route and per-key rate limits with token buckets. You can set burst size and sustained rates in the Console.

[11:05] Miguel: What about data residency — any EU/US region options?
[11:09] Hannah: Hosted has regional control; we deploy in US and EU regions. Private allows on-prem if needed. For PHI you'd likely want dedicated or private long-term.

[11:25] Priya: Will Optimize recommend quantization profiles?
[11:29] Hannah: Yes Optimize analyzes workload and suggests quantization or smaller model variants when cost reduction keeps quality within thresholds. It will produce expected latency and cost deltas per suggestion.

[11:45] Miguel: Can you run a small benchmark for us? Like 1000 synthetic triage prompts?
[11:49] Jordan: Absolutely. For the pilot we'll propose a 7-day run with a synthetic harness you provide or we can generate. We'll produce token-level latency and quality evals.

[12:05] Priya: What metrics will you report?
[12:08] Hannah: Latency p50/p95/p99, tokens per second, cost per 1k requests, quality via a holdout prompt set (accuracy/precision for clinical intents), and error/failure rates.

[12:25] Miguel: Any limitations on streaming for very long responses?
[12:29] Samir: Longer responses stream fine but tail latency may increase. You can chunk outputs or request streaming checkpoints. For very long outputs we sometimes prefer async generation endpoints.

[12:48] Ellen: Can the Console show per-user cost?
[12:51] Jordan: Yes, per-token billing broken down by route, token type, and you can tag requests for attribution.

[13:05] Priya: One last question: will pilot data be used to train models?
[13:10] Hannah: No. Hosted accounts can be configured so customer content is not used for training. We'll include explicit language in the pilot agreement.

--- Recap & Next steps ---
[13:30] Jordan: Quick recap: we'll send SOC2/security pack, sample pilot pricing and onboarding, and two benchmark configs. Customer will confirm dataset and concurrency expectations. Then we'll schedule a bench/run review.
[13:45] Miguel: Sounds good. We'll aim to have prompt set and concurrency numbers by the 18th.
[13:50] Priya: We'll also try one quick POC integration in our sandbox to verify streaming UI.
[13:55] Ellen: Great, thanks everyone.
[14:00] Jordan: Thanks for your time — we'll follow up with the docs and dates.

Notes about transcription: Some vendor/product names were auto-transcribed (e.g., "red wood" vs "Redwood") and a few technical terms may be imperfect (e.g., KV cache sometimes appears as "K V cash"). We will attach the call recording and console screenshots in the follow-up.
